message.content:
I don’t have real‑time data, but you can quickly check the current air quality in Los Angeles by visiting one of the following resources:

| Source | What it offers | How to use |
|--------|----------------|------------|
| **AirNow** (airnow.gov) | Official EPA air‑quality index (AQI) for all U.S. cities, plus pollutant breakdowns (PM₂.₅, PM₁₀, O₃, NO₂, CO). | Enter “Los Angeles” in the search box or use the map. |
| **AQICN** (aqicn.org) | Global AQI with real‑time data, forecasts, and health recommendations. | Search “Los Angeles” or use the mobile app. |
| **Local news sites** (e.g., LA Times, KABC) | Often publish live updates during smog events. | Look for “air quality” or “smog” sections. |
| **Weather apps** (Weather.com, AccuWeather, Weather Underground) | Many include an AQI widget. | Open the app, search for Los Angeles, and scroll to the “Air Quality” section. |

If you’re planning outdoor activities, the EPA’s AirNow site also provides health advice based on the AQI level:

- **0–50 (Good)** – No special precautions needed.  
- **51–100 (Moderate)** – Sensitive groups (children, elderly, people with respiratory issues) may want to reduce prolonged exertion.  
- **101–150 (Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups)** – Sensitive groups should limit outdoor exertion.  
- **151–200 (Unhealthy)** – Everyone should reduce prolonged outdoor activity.  
- **201–300 (Very Unhealthy)** – Avoid outdoor exertion; consider staying indoors.  
- **301+ (Hazardous)** – Stay indoors and keep windows closed; use air purifiers if possible.

For the most accurate, up‑to‑minute reading, check the AirNow or AQICN sites right now.
